output.text_response:
This is not a real conflict. The two dates are the same day written in two different year-numbering systems.

**Why they differ:** Bolton-le-Moors was in England, where the civil year began on 25 March until 1752. Under that Old Style convention, a date falling between 1 January and 24 March was counted in the *previous* year. The calendar conversion confirms that 14 February 1746 (Old Style) is exactly 14 February 1747 (New Style/modern). The original register used the Old Style year, and the printed transcript modernised it to 1747. The day, month, parish, and father are identical — there is no factual disagreement at all.

**On source independence:** The printed transcript is a derivative copy of the same register page, so it cannot independently corroborate the register. These count as one source, not two.

**What to record:**

- **Best form:** `14 February 1746/7` — the double-date notation standard for English Old Style dates. Note that the register reads 1746 under the Old Style year beginning 25 March.
- **If your software requires a single year:** Use **1747** (modern equivalent) and note it is the modern rendering of the register's 1746.
- Keep **a_001** (the original register) as the primary evidence; treat **a_002** (the printed transcript) as its transcription.

No conflict resolution entry is needed.

agent_returns.text:
This is not a real conflict. The two dates are the same day written in two year-numbering systems, so no conflict entry is needed.

Bolton-le-Moors was in England, where the civil year began on 25 March until 1752. Under that system, a date from 1 January to 24 March is counted in the previous year when the year is written in the modern way. The calendar tool confirms that 14 February 1746 in the old-style count is 14 February 1747 in the modern count. The register wrote 1746, and the printed transcript modernised it to 1747. Its own note says the day, month, parish and father all match.

The transcript also cannot corroborate the register. It is a derivative copy of the same page, so it counts as one source, not two.

For the record, use the original register's form, which is also the most defensible: **14 February 1746/7**, with the note that the register reads 1746 under the old-style year that began 25 March. If your software only accepts one year, use 1747 and state that it is the modern-style equivalent of the register's 1746. Either way, keep a_001 as the primary evidence and treat a_002 as its transcription.

The conflict-resolution agent analysed the case and recorded it as **conflict c_001 (unresolved, identity conflict)**, blocking parentage question q_001. Here is its full finding:

---

**Identity conflict: Anders Pedersen (1875 census) vs. your Anders Hansen (a_001, a_002)**

**Current assessment — probably different persons, but not yet resolved.**

The key signal is the patronymic. In 1875 Norway (before the 1923 surname law), surnames worked as patronymics:
- **Pedersen** = son of Peder
- **Hansen** = son of Hans

Your subject's surname and his father in the tree (Hans Olsen) both point to a father named Hans. The census entry's patronymic Pedersen points to a father named Peder — a different man. This is the strongest differentiator in the Norwegian naming system.

The matching given name, age, and parish district are **not** sufficient to override this — Anders was a common name, and in a rural district there would routinely be multiple boys of similar age with the same given name.

**What would resolve it:**
1. **The 1875 census page image** — to check whether the index entry "Pedersen" is a transcription/indexing error (scribal slip or indexer mistake), and to identify the actual household head.
2. **A Ringsaker baptismal register** — a record naming Anders's father as either Hans or Peder would settle it definitively.
3. **An earlier census (1865)** — placing your Anders in a household headed by Hans Olsen would confirm they are different people.

A record placing your Anders in that specific census household would flip the verdict to "same person." Absent that, the different patronymic strongly favors these being two distinct boys.

**Recommended next step:** Search the baptism registers and 1865 census for Ringsaker to find a record that names Anders's father.

They are not independent of each other in the way that would make them corroborate. The index is a clerk's alphabetical derivative of marriage papers, and the name in it was copied by a clerk from a source we do not hold, so it is at best one remote witness to the mother's name. The birth act reading is itself a single item: one informant (the father, a household member) and one handwritten entry. The 'Jannetje' reading of the groom's mother on the same act is a different person's name and does not corroborate the mother's reading. Nothing in the file shows that the index's clerk had access to the birth act, so the two cannot be treated as one unit, but neither is an independent check on the first letter, which is the only point in dispute.
fields.weighing_analysis: The disputed item is the first letter of the mother's given name (J, T or F with 'annetje' fixed). The birth act is the closer record to the event (a birth, 1828, informant the father who lived in the household) and is an original, so on relevance, category and informant proximity it has the edge. Its weakness is legibility: the first letter is unclear, the OCR read J, and the researcher reads T, so the act's reading is contested on consistency and clarity. The marriage index is a secondary, clerk-made derivative, decades removed from a birth, and it names the mother only in passing. Those factors favour the birth act if its letter can be read, but they do not settle the letter itself. Neither side can be preferred on the present file: the only reading that is firsthand is the one the researcher cannot confirm.
fields.resolution_rationale: The problem is the given name of Cornelis van Noord's mother, which decides which woman the parentage question names (q_001). Two records give the name: the 1828 birth act, where the father reported the mother's name and the first letter is unclear on the handwritten page (read as J by the machine transcription, as T by the researcher), and the 1838-1848 ten-year marriage index, which gives 'Fannetje van Noord'. The birth act is the closer record, made at the birth by a household informant, and it is the original. The index is a clerk's later derivative, and its clerk was not present at the birth. The index's reading agrees with neither 'J' nor 'T' on the first letter of the act, so it cannot break the tie. The index error, if any, is a copying slip of the clerk, which is the usual fault of alphabetical marriage indexes; and the first letter of the act is the reading most at risk from the handwriting and from the machine transcription. Neither reading can be preferred until the act's first letter is read directly from the page image, so the conflict stays open. The decisive records are: a direct, unassisted reading of the 1828 birth act image for the first letter; the birth or marriage act of a sibling of Cornelis in the same Zuid-Holland registry, which names the mother in the same hand; and the marriage act itself, not only its index entry, if it names the mother. No record already in the file settles it.

fields.independence_analysis: The 1850 census entry (a_001) and the 1908 death certificate (a_011, a_013) come from different creators and different informants: the enumerator's household informant in 1850, and a son-in-law (James Brown) reporting what he was told in 1908. The 1860 census (a_010) is a third record with its own enumeration. The fact that links the death certificate to the 1850 household, the father's name Thomas Flynn, is supplied by an informant outside the 1850 household, so agreement between the two is corroboration rather than a restatement of one source. The rival Patrick of household 197 has no assertion of its own in the file, so it rests only on the conflict description.
fields.weighing_analysis: Decisive factors: (1) Consistency of identifying details. The 1850 Patrick (age 5) sits in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household, and the 1908 death certificate names Thomas Flynn as father of a man of the right age who died in Schuylkill County. Both records name the same father and the same county. (2) Continuity. The 1860 census places a Patrick aged 15 in the same Thomas Flynn household in the same county, so the household link persists across two enumerations. (3) Directness and relevance. The death certificate directly names the father, which is the fact the identity question depends on. Nothing in the file places a Patrick Flynn with a different father in Schuylkill County, and the description's household 197 Patrick is unsupported by any recorded assertion. Weaknesses: the 1850 entry is inferred from household position, and the death certificate informant was not present for the family's early life.
fields.resolution_rationale: The problem is whether the Patrick Flynn in Thomas Flynn's 1850 household is the same man whose 1908 death certificate names Thomas Flynn as father. The answer decides whether the 1850 and 1860 records can be used at all for the parentage question. The 1850 census (a_001), recorded by an enumerator from a household informant, shows Patrick, age 5, in Thomas Flynn's household in Schuylkill County. The 1908 death certificate (a_013), supplied by a son-in-law who was not present for the family's early years, names Thomas Flynn as father. The 1860 census (a_010) shows a Patrick aged 15 in the same household. The identity is supported by two informants outside the 1850 enumeration, the death certificate's father and the 1860 household, and no record of the file places a Patrick with a different father in the county. The rival household-197 Patrick has no recorded assertion, so it cannot keep the conflict open once the subject is placed. The son-in-law's report of parentage is secondhand, and the 1850 household entry is an inference, so residual doubt is noted, but the elimination is positive. The same-named Patrick in household 197 is a possibility that the existing records do not show; the identity rests on the father-name link the death certificate supplies, which the son-in-law had from family talk rather than direct knowledge. The name Thomas Flynn is a common one, so this link is the weakest point and should be re-checked if a record for household 197 is found.
